Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Conflict: Confrontations, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Vignette:
James is a 36-year-old North American male who serves as a tax consultant in a bustling downtown office. Married and a veteran of the military, James has found that his service experiences have left indelible marks on his daily life. His PTSD symptoms emerged after a particularly harrowing deployment where he witnessed intense conflict and several close calls with death. The traumatic event began during a routine patrol when an unexpected explosion rocked their convoy. Amidst the chaos, James saw fellow soldiers injured and heard screams that seemed to echo through every corner of his mind. The taste of dust and gunpowder filled his mouth as he rushed to assist the wounded. This experience has left him deeply scarred, particularly by certain triggers like confrontations and specific conversation topics. James had come to believe that any form of physical contact with others was a potential threat. He would react with alarm if someone touched him unexpectedly, often pulling away reflexively. In his office, James found himself frequently startled when colleagues accidentally brushed past him or patted him on the back in camaraderie. These interactions left him feeling shaken and anxious, leading to avoidance behaviors that strained relationships at work. One day, while attending a mandatory team-building retreat, an unexpected handshake from a new colleague triggered an acute anxiety response. James felt his heart race and sweat form beads on his forehead. He quickly excused himself, retreating to the nearest bathroom where he could regroup and calm down. This incident marked one of many instances where James felt compelled to avoid any positive emotions because they made him feel unsafe. James had developed a habit of pushing away positive feelings due to a pervasive sense that something dangerous was always around the corner. He often found himself feeling numb, as if he were an observer rather than a participant in his own life. This emotional disconnection extended into his marriage, where he avoided deep conversations or meaningful interactions with his wife. In his daily routine, James would meticulously plan his days to include escape routes wherever he went. Whether it was the office building or a crowded coffee shop, he would carefully note every exit and entrance, feeling only secure once he had identified these potential escape paths. This behavior became particularly pronounced in public spaces where unexpected silence made him feel as if danger were imminent. James often experienced vivid flashbacks of the traumatic event, which were triggered by certain tastes that reminded him of the dust and gunpowder from the explosion. These memories would flood his mind with overwhelming emotions, leaving him feeling paralyzed and unable to continue his work or engage in social activities. At other times, he would recall the events but feel completely numb, as if they had happened to someone else. The impact on his marriage was significant. James avoided talking about the event or its aftermath with his wife, who felt increasingly isolated and disconnected from him. This avoidance not only strained their relationship but also exacerbated his own sense of isolation and fear. What finally brought James to seek help was a combination of escalating symptoms and the realization that he could no longer avoid the triggers that surrounded him daily. He had come to believe that if he continued on this path, his life would be forever compromised by his trauma. His greatest hope was to regain some sense of control over his emotions and relationships, to find a way to reconnect with his wife and colleagues without feeling perpetually threatened. In therapy, James expressed the fear that he might never fully recover from the event or that it could always intrude into his life unexpectedly. He hoped to learn strategies for managing his triggers and finding ways to engage in positive emotions again, reclaiming some sense of normalcy in his daily life.
